Hairstyle Ideas

Short Hairstyles

Home / Hairstyles / Short Hairstyles

Short styles range from close-cropped pixies to chin-length bobs, and they tend to show off haircut precision more than longer styles do — there's simply less hair to hide an uneven line, which is why regular trims matter more to keep the shape sharp. Going short is also one of the more committed style changes you can make, so it's worth understanding the options and the upkeep involved before booking the first cut.

Popular Short Styles

  • Classic pixie cut: short all over with soft, textured layers on top — a versatile option that works across most hair textures.
  • Textured crop: a slightly longer, choppier take on the pixie with more length left on top for styling flexibility.
  • Blunt bob: a single, even length that hits at or above the chin, prized for its graphic, clean line.
  • Asymmetrical bob: intentionally uneven length, often shorter in the back and longer in the front, for a more modern silhouette.
  • Shag: heavily layered, textured, and deliberately undone-looking — lower-maintenance day to day than a blunt style.

Is a Short Cut Right for Your Hair Type?

Straight and wavy hair generally show off precise short shapes well, since the cut's lines stay visible. Curly and coily hair can absolutely be worn short too, but the cut needs to account for how much the hair shrinks once it dries and curls up — a stylist experienced with curly hair will typically cut it dry to see the true, settled shape before finalizing length.

The Growing-Out Period

One thing worth planning for before you go short: the growing-out phase. Most short cuts go through an awkward stage somewhere between three and six months as length starts to return unevenly. Talking to your stylist about this ahead of time — and scheduling shaping trims through that stretch — makes the transition much smoother than trying to grow it out with no plan at all.

Upkeep

Plan on a trim roughly every 4–6 weeks to maintain shape, since short cuts grow out of their line more visibly than longer styles — even a small amount of extra length can noticeably change how a precise short cut sits. Styling is often faster day to day than with long hair, which is one of the appeals, but the haircut itself needs more frequent professional attention to stay sharp.

Talking to Your Stylist About Going Short

If you've never worn your hair this short, ask your stylist to walk through the process in stages rather than committing to the shortest version all at once, if you're hesitant. Many stylists are happy to do an intermediate cut first so you can get a feel for a shorter length before going all the way.

Styling Short Hair Day to Day

One underrated benefit of going short: daily styling is usually much faster. A pixie or crop often needs just a small amount of texturizing product worked through damp hair and a quick blast with a dryer, compared to the longer routines longer styles typically require. That time savings is part of why many people who go short once end up returning to it again in the future, even after growing it out for a change of pace.

Accessorizing Short Hair

Short styles limit some accessory options — a lot of hairpins and clips need more length to anchor into — but headbands, small decorative pins, and scarves all work well and can add variety without growing anything out. If you're missing the ability to change your look day to day, small accessories are often the easiest way to add variation to a short cut.
